Instead of asking players to make that decision before creating a character, World of Warcraft: Forever is going realmless, making it easier to connect with friends while still preserving the community feel that has always made realms memorable.
Rather than choosing from a long list of realms, players will choose a ruleset that matches how they want to experience Azeroth:
Normal: The baseline World of Warcraft experience with a focus on cooperation, where player-versus-player combat requires mutual consent
PvP: For players who want every trip into contested territory to carry more danger, excitement, and world conflict.
Roleplaying: For players who want to lean more deeply into the fantasy of Azeroth and seek out like-minded adventurers.
Hardcore: Available after launch for players seeking the ultimate challenge, where every decision matters and death carries lasting consequences.

As part of the server updates, characters will also use two-part names, similar to having a “first name” and “last name.” Because names will be unique per region, this gives players more room to create original character names, such as “Ana Forever,” while keeping those identities recognizable acros
Players will also be able to choose a language preference and encounter others who share that preference.

Players can visit a transmogrifier in certain cities to configure transmogrified outfits or disable the system entirely. In practical terms, opting out means players will only see others around them as they are, in their equipped gear.

For epic raid drops, appearances are granted on acquisition only to the player the item binds to, preserving the prestige of higher-level rewards and leaving organized loot decisions in the hands of raid groups.
Transmogrification still follows item-type rules, so plate transmogs to plate and cloth transmogs to cloth.

Disabling the system does not prevent players from configuring and displaying their own transmog if they want to hide a specific slot such as a helm or cloak or show a particular appearance without enabling the full system for themselves.
That philosophy shows up in the pace of play. A solo player can expect an ordinary creature to take roughly 10–15 seconds to defeat, giving individual pulls room to matter.

New stats broaden those choices further. Some items can reduce the chance for attacks to be parried or dodged, while spellcaster-oriented weapons now grant spell damage and healing so spellcasters can look forward to level-up weapons in the same way Warriors, Rogues, and Hunters do.
Trinkets are being pushed toward more varied, situational effects, with examples such as the Worgenbane Talisman showing how different trinkets can matter in different circumstances.
Quest rewards have also been updated or expanded to support more classes and roles.

The system expands the simple Cooking Fire from the Cooking profession into a Basic Campfire.
Placing a campfire creates a campsite where players can rest and gain access to useful benefits such as vendors, repairs, profession workspaces, and one-hour buffs.
A Basic Campfire allows up to three special crafted objects to be added by nearby players. Every profession has three different objects learned at different skill levels.

The first campsite objects are learned once a profession reaches skill level 20, either from special nonplayer characters (NPCs) who introduce players to camping or from profession trainers, while more advanced objects come from Blueprint recipes that drop from specific dungeon bosses.
